strengths: Identifies and quantitatively analyzes a structural failure mode of linear RoPE interpolation in mixed-resolution diffusion transformers: cross-resolution attention mixes incompatible RoPE phase rates, causing aliasing and attention collapse.

Proposes Cross-Resolution Phase-Aligned Attention (CRPA), a simple, training-free, drop-in fix that re-indexes all key/value RoPE positions to the query's stride so that a single attention operation compares phases on one consistent scale.
Introduces a lightweight Boundary Expand-and-Replace module to smooth LR-HR transitions, with an ablation showing it improves boundary coherence.

Provides strong empirical evidence on large models: Wan2.1-1.3B for text-to-video and FLUX.1-dev for text-to-image, comparing against multiple interpolation baselines (PI-LR, PI-HR, NTK, PI+NTK, YaRN) and metrics (DOVER, VBench, FID, CLIP-IQA, MUSIQ, CLIP).
Demonstrates substantial efficiency gains: CRPA adds only ~0.3% latency overhead, and the method approaches high-resolution-only quality at much lower cost (e.g., 43s vs 172s for video).

Supplement includes a derivation of the kernel decomposition, additional comparisons under fixed compute budgets, three-stage comparisons against RALU/Bottleneck/ToCa, ablation of boundary padding, overhead breakdown, and a limitations discussion.
weaknesses: The CRPA formulation p_k^(q)=alpha p_k assumes aligned origins or global coordinates; for arbitrary mixed-resolution layouts with region offsets, the mapping may need an affine offset as in the piecewise-affine map discussed in Sec. 3.2, and this is not fully formalized in the main method.

The notation 'native grid spacing' versus the scale ratio alpha = S_q/S_k is potentially confusing, since in the examples the scale factor behaves like a sampling-rate ratio rather than a spacing ratio.

The empirical analysis of attention score vs. relative distance ignores softmax normalization; Eq. (6) is an approximation over pairwise pre-softmax scores, not a formal proof that softmax attention necessarily collapses.

Boundary Expand-and-Replace relies on a learned latent up/downsampler and a saliency detector (DeepGazeIIE); the training/provenance of the 25M resizer is not fully specified, and the saliency-based region selection is not ablated, so the full pipeline is not entirely training-free.

Experiments are limited to two base models (Wan2.1-1.3B and FLUX.1-dev) and specific tasks; generalizability to other DiTs, larger models, and more extreme mixed-resolution layouts remains to be established.

The abstract/claim of 'outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods' is somewhat overbroad: gains are mainly over RoPE interpolation baselines in mixed-resolution denoising, while high-resolution-only baselines still achieve higher fidelity on some metrics.
No code release is mentioned, which may limit reproducibility despite the detailed supplement.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically relevant setting: mixed-resolution denoising in pretrained DiTs, where naive RoPE interpolation is indeed brittle.

The core idea of CRPA (expressing all key/value phases on the query's stride so equal physical distances yield equal phase increments) is simple, well-motivated, and cheap; the overhead table (Table 9) shows CRPA adds only ~0.3% latency, which is a real practical advantage.

The paper does a reasonable job of presenting the failure mode both qualitatively (Figs. 1, 2, 6, 12) and via a head-level probing analysis (Fig. 3) plus a sinusoidal kernel decomposition (Eq. 6 and Supp. A) that at least offers an interpretable account of the mechanism.

Experiments are broad: two base models (Wan2.1-1.3B video, FLUX.1-dev image), multiple RoPE-interpolation baselines (PI-LR, PI-HR, NTK, PI+NTK, YARN, RALU), standard benchmarks (VBench, DOVER, FID, CLIP-IQA, MUSIQ, CLIP), plus ablations on the Boundary Expand-and-Replace band size and combinations with orthogonal accelerators (TeaCache, MagCache, ToCa).
The Boundary Expand-and-Replace module is a sensible engineering addition, and the ablation in Table 8 shows a non-trivial VBench gain (0.747 → 0.770).
weaknesses: The causal claim that 'phase aliasing' is the driver of the failure is supported mainly by correlational observations (sharp peak of κ(Δ) near Δ≈0, periodicity) rather than by an intervention that isolates phase mismatch from the confounding effects of index rescaling. The claim that 'tiny cross-rate inconsistencies reliably cause blur, artifacts, or full collapse' is stronger than what Fig. 3 shows, and the reported periodicity (~2–3 index units) is not obviously catastrophic at the resampling factors used.

The empirical gains are modest where they matter most. On image generation (Table 2) Ours 32.04 FID vs YARN 33.83, and Ours is still worse than the full-HR baseline (31.50). In the three-stage setting (Table 3) Ours-18 32.45 vs RALU-18 32.91, a 0.46 FID improvement. The paper's framing of 'outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods' overstates the case: the comparison set is RoPE-interpolation variants for mixed-resolution denoising, not the broader SOTA for image/video generation.

The 'training-free' framing is overstated. The Boundary Expand-and-Replace step depends on a trained latent up/downsampler (25M params for Wan, 6M for FLUX), a tiny VAE, and a pretrained saliency model (DeepGazeIIE). Only the base DiT is frozen. The claim of being 'fully compatible with pretrained DiTs' should be qualified.

For LR queries attending to HR keys, CRPA compresses/subsamples HR tokens (e.g., [6,7,8,9]→[3,4]), which discards HR content. The paper does not analyze this information loss, nor does it justify why this is preferable to, e.g., simply restricting cross-resolution attention or computing pairwise physical offsets with explicit per-pair scaling.

Several results are not explained and invite suspicion of metric artifacts or noise. In Table 1 the proposed method (VBench total 0.770) exceeds the full-HR baseline (0.766) and the 480p→960p upper-bound reference (0.762), while being worse on DOVER Aesthetic/Technical. The paper does not discuss why mixed-resolution denoising should beat full-HR denoising; absent an explanation this undermines confidence in the quantitative story.

The analysis in Sec. 3.3 borrows the RoPE-dominance score from [15] and then uses it to define which heads show the effect, which is close to circular; the 'amplification in RoPE-dominant heads' observation largely follows from the definition rather than being an independent finding.

Qualitative results still show residual artifacts (e.g., the panda/swing-set row in Fig. 6 and the face in Fig. 6/12 under 'Ours'), so the practical robustness claim is not fully borne out by the visual evidence.

Novelty is incremental: the mechanism is essentially per-attention-call normalization of relative positional offsets, a small variant on standard relative position handling, and the paper does not position it against conceptually simpler alternatives that avoid the problem altogether.

Presentation: some claims in the abstract and intro (e.g., 'full collapse', 'state-of-the-art') are not matched by the evidence, and the writing occasionally conflates the fixed mechanism (CRPA) with the engineered pipeline (saliency-based region selection + resizers).

strengths: The paper identifies and characterizes a concrete, previously unexplored failure mode of RoPE positional interpolation in mixed-resolution DiT denoising. The diagnostic in Sec. 3.3 is well designed: measuring content-averaged query-key cosine similarity as a function of relative offset Delta (Fig. 3) reveals a sharp near-zero peak, strong multi-frequency periodicity, and amplification in RoPE-dominant heads that is stable across diffusion timesteps, supporting the claim of a pretrained 'phase prior' rather than a transient artifact. The complementary failure modes of PI-LR (plausible LR, collapsed HR) and PI-HR (collapsed LR, plausible HR) in Fig. 2 provide a nice controlled counterexample.

The proposed fix (CRPA) is simple, principled, and well motivated by the analysis: expressing all key/value positions on the query's grid before applying RoPE so that equal physical distances always yield identical phase increments. The decomposition in Eq. 6 (and its derivation in Sec. A) is exact and gives a clean interpretation of the attention score as a content-weighted mixture of sinusoids at the fixed RoPE frequencies, which is a genuinely useful way to reason about the failure mode. The method is drop-in, requires negligible overhead (Table 9: CRPA ~0.3% of runtime), and preserves the pretrained model.

The empirical evidence spans two strong, modern base models (Wan2.1-1.3B for video, FLUX.1-dev for image) and multiple metrics (VBench/DOVER for video; FID/CLIP-IQA/MUSIQ/CLIP for images), and the method consistently outperforms the mixed-resolution RoPE interpolation baselines (PI-LR, PI-HR, NTK, PI+NTK, YARN) at large speedups (43s vs 131s/172s). The comparison against RALU, Bottleneck Sampling, and ToCa under matched 4x/7x acceleration budgets (Table 7) is a meaningful, non-trivial baseline set, and the quality-cost curve over the HR token ratio (Fig. 9) is informative.

Experimental hygiene is generally good: ablations of the boundary module and the overlap band width (Table 8), a per-component overhead breakdown (Table 9), combination with orthogonal acceleration methods (Tables 4 and 5), matched-budget comparison against full-HR denoising (Table 6), detailed per-metric VBench breakdowns (Table 10), and a discussion of limitations (ultra-high-resolution instability) plus released prompts.

The paper is clearly written, the figures (e.g., Fig. 4's index-space illustration, Fig. 6/7/12's side-by-side comparisons) communicate the failure mode and the fix effectively, and the method addresses a practically important problem (efficient mixed-resolution DiT inference).
weaknesses: The headline framing ('outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods') is somewhat inflated by the choice of baselines: PI-LR, PI-HR, NTK, and YARN are shown to essentially collapse or produce severe artifacts, so beating them is a weak test. The more meaningful comparisons in Table 1 (HR: 79.12 DOVER Overall; LR+HR reference: 74.88) and Table 2 (HR: CLIP-IQA 0.640, MUSIQ 71.48) show that the method is only marginally above the two-stage LR+HR reference (75.34 vs 74.88) and still clearly below full-HR on several metrics (Aesthetic 99.63 vs 99.83, Technical 10.01 vs 10.43, CLIP-IQA 0.563 vs 0.640, MUSIQ 68.88 vs 71.48). The claim that quality is 'close to the high-resolution-only baseline' holds for some metrics but not all, and the paper does not analyze this gap.

The ablation in Table 8 indicates that a large share of the headline gain comes from the Boundary Expand-and-Replace module rather than from CRPA itself: CRPA alone (n_pad = 0,0) yields 68.43 DOVER Overall, while adding the boundary band (2,2) raises it to 75.34 (Quality 0.781 -> 0.808, Semantics 0.614 -> 0.622). This is a large jump for a component described as 'lightweight' and it is analyzed only qualitatively (Fig. 10) plus one band-size sweep. Given that the paper's narrative and title center on the phase-alignment principle, this imbalance deserves more scrutiny (e.g., why does content exchange at boundaries help so much if the failure is positional, and does the boundary module alone on top of PI-LR recover much of the gain?).

The 'training-free' characterization is only partially accurate. The Boundary Expand-and-Replace step relies on a learned latent up/downsampler (Sec. 4.2; ~25M parameters per resizer for Wan2.1 and ~6M for FLUX, per Sec. C), and the training data, objective, and procedure for these resizers are not reported. Since these modules are applied at every diffusion step and contribute substantially to the final numbers, the omission is a reproducibility gap and weakens the drop-in claim.

The core mechanism is conceptually modest in novelty: CRPA is essentially 'express every position in a single, common unit (the query's grid) before applying RoPE.' The paper's real contribution is the diagnosis that existing interpolation schemes deviate from this and the quantification of why the deviation is catastrophic, which is valuable, but a reader may reasonably ask whether the fix itself would be the default implementation choice.

Some diagnostic details are under-specified. The Delta-score curve kappa(Delta) is estimated by randomly sampling token pairs from forward passes and averaging over content; it is unclear how sampling bias in the pair distribution affects the estimated curve, especially at large |Delta|. The RoPE-dominance threshold (rds > 0.085) is asserted without justification. It would strengthen the causal story to show that applying CRPA alone restores the pretrained kappa(Delta) profile of the affected heads, and to rule out the competing explanation that cross-resolution attention fails mainly because low- and high-resolution token content statistics are incompatible (the complementary PI-LR/PI-HR failure modes argue for the phase explanation, but this is not tested directly).

Evaluation breadth and rigor are limited in a few respects: only two base models are tested, no seed/variance or significance information is reported for any metric, and there is no mention of a code release, which is relevant given the multiple learned and external components (tiny VAE, DeepGazeIIE saliency model, learned resizers, importance-based region selection). The importance-based region-selection pipeline also introduces an extra dependency whose effect on the reported numbers is not ablated.

strengths: Provides a clear and useful diagnosis of why RoPE position interpolation fails in mixed-resolution diffusion transformers: the attention similarity follows a periodic/sinusoidal function of relative distance, so no single global rescaling can preserve pre-trained positional scales. The analysis is supported by empirical κ(Δ) curves and a theoretical mixture-of-sinusoids interpretation.

Proposes Phase-Aligned Mixed-Resolution Attention (PMA), a simple and largely training-free mechanism that aligns key positions to each query's native resolution scale before attention. It directly targets the identified root cause and requires no architectural changes, with reported low overhead.

Introduces the Boundary Expand-and-Replace module and a coarse-to-fine saliency-guided pipeline, further improving local coherence around LR-HR transitions and enabling practical mixed-resolution image/video generation.

Conducts extensive experiments on large-scale diffusion models (Wan2.1-1.3B and FLUX.1-dev) with multiple metrics and baselines, including comparisons against RoPE interpolation variants and diffusion acceleration methods. Shows strong quality-speed trade-offs and broad applicability, including integration with orthogonal acceleration techniques and multi-resolution extensions.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear contributions, informative figures, and an explicit limitations section that acknowledges remaining failure cases and future directions.
weaknesses: Although PMA itself is training-free, the full pipeline relies on a trained latent up/downsampler for BER and an off-the-shelf saliency model for region selection, so the overall system is not fully training-free; the paper's framing could be more precise about this.

Experimental results do not consistently surpass the high-resolution baseline across all metrics: for example, DOVER overall and ImageReward are lower than HR in several settings, meaning the main practical gain is efficiency at comparable rather than uniformly superior quality. Claims of state-of-the-art results should be qualified accordingly.

There is no direct controlled comparison with RALU under identical mixed-resolution settings, despite it being the closest prior work; this makes the empirical claim of being the first to focus on mixed-resolution generation somewhat less definitive.

The theoretical analysis assumes a periodic κ(Δ) structure and measures it in pretrained models; while supported by a supplement, the expected-cosine-similarity measurement may still be influenced by content correlations among sampled tokens, and the derivation focuses on a single-head sinusoidal mixture rather than the full multi-head, multi-axis DiT attention behavior.

Practical implementation details for the modified attention grouping (HR queries vs. LR queries) and reproducibility are not fully provided; no code or project-page link is visible in the manuscript, although the method section and supplement are reasonably detailed.

strengths: Identifies and analyzes an important practical issue: RoPE's periodic relative-distance bias causes instability when mixing token resolutions in diffusion transformers.
Proposes a simple inference-time mechanism, PMA, that re-indexes key positions to the query's native resolution, plus a BER module to reduce boundary artifacts.
Provides experiments on both image (FLUX.1-dev) and video (Wan2.1) DiTs, with multiple metrics, ablations, multi-resolution scaling, and integration with acceleration methods.
weaknesses: The key empirical evidence for the RoPE scale bias (κ(Δ)) is not fully convincing: if q and k are truly random independent normalized vectors, the expected dot product is zero; the reported nonzero sinusoidal curves likely reflect content/architecture biases rather than pure RoPE positional bias. The paper does not adequately isolate positional effects.

The theory (Eq. 6) has content-dependent coefficients, so averaging over random token pairs cannot isolate positional bias. The RoPE-only baseline in the supplement needs more explanation and controls to support the central claim.

PMA's per-query rescaling does not establish a single consistent positional scale; it creates asymmetric, scale-dependent attention with no formal guarantee. The claim of enforcing a consistent scale for every query-key pair is overstated.

The method is not fully training-free: BER requires training latent up/downsamplers (25M/6M parameters) on external datasets, adding complexity and model-specific dependence that is not well evaluated.

Experimental results are mixed and overclaimed: in Table 1 Ours trails the HR baseline in DOVER overall (75.34 vs 79.12), and in Table 2 ImgReward is lower (0.978 vs 1.062), yet the paper claims state-of-the-art fidelity and substantial detail gain. Human evaluation is absent.

Efficiency claims relative to mixed-resolution baselines are unclear: Ours takes 43.2s, identical to PI-LR, so the main gain is quality, not speed. Baselines such as YaRN, NTK, and acceleration methods may not be fully tuned, and the rds>0.085 threshold appears arbitrary.

Novelty is incremental: mixed-resolution tokenization and variable-resolution attention have been explored before, and the 'first to focus on mixed-resolution generation' claim is too strong. Relevant prior work is not sufficiently discussed or compared.
Reproducibility is limited: the project page URL is blank, no code/models are released, and key training details for BER rely on external datasets. This makes exact reproduction difficult.

strengths: The diagnosis of RoPE-related failure in mixed-resolution DiT attention is well-motivated and novel. The empirical characterization of the sinusoidal scale bias κ(Δ) across time/height/width axes and diffusion timesteps (Fig. 3, Figs. 15, 16, 24) is a genuinely informative piece of analysis that clarifies why RoPE position interpolation fails under mixed resolution.

The proposed Phase-Aligned Mixed-Resolution Attention (PMA) is simple, elegant, and effectively motivated by the analysis: rescaling key positions into each query's native grid so that every query-key pair is evaluated at the phase the pretrained head was calibrated to. This is a clean design that is easy to implement on pretrained models.

The empirical evidence is broad and consistent. Experiments cover both a video model (Wan2.1-1.3B) and an image model (FLUX.1-dev), report multiple metrics (DOVER, VBench, ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, MUSIQ, CLIP), and show clear gains over PI-LR, PI-HR, NTK, PI+NTK, and YaRN. The 3-way and 4-way mixed-resolution tables (Tabs. 8, 9, 13, 14; Tabs. 11, 12) further strengthen the case.

The paper convincingly demonstrates composability with orthogonal acceleration methods (TeaCache, MagCache, DMD, FLUX.1-schnell), and provides a useful overhead breakdown (Tab. 16) showing PMA, tiny VAE, and saliency model are all inexpensive.

Robustness is carefully checked: the method performs well across multiple saliency models and even with a fixed center square (Tab. 6), and HR-key handling for LR queries is ablated (Tab. 15). The BER ablation (Fig. 11, Tab. 7) and npad sweep are useful.

The limitations section is candid (Fig. 17), and the paper honestly acknowledges that the strategy fits naturally with saliency-guided coarse-to-fine denoising, positioning the contribution as orthogonal to the choice of region localizer.

The idea of aligning RoPE phases per query-key pair is practical and could generalize beyond this paper's specific settings, which is a meaningful contribution to the diffusion-acceleration community.
weaknesses: The core mechanism (PMA) is conceptually straightforward: it is essentially a per-query relative RoPE where the key's position is reindexed to the query's native grid. Once the diagnosis is established, the fix is close to immediate. The main scientific contribution therefore rests more on the diagnostic analysis than on the algorithmic novelty of PMA itself.

The 'training-free' framing is somewhat overstated in places. While PMA itself is training-free, the overall pipeline depends on trained latent up/downsamplers (6–25M params, Tab. 16) in the Boundary Expand-and-Replace module and on off-the-shelf saliency predictors. This should be made clear in the abstract/intro rather than only in the method section.

The claim that this is 'the first work to focus on mixed-resolution generation' is not accurate—RALU [44] explicitly uses mixed resolution, and the paper effectively acknowledges this in the same sentence. The claim should be softened to the specific RoPE-related contribution.

Comparison against generic diffusion acceleration methods (TeaCache, MagCache, ToMe, UniPC, DPM++) is somewhat apples-to-oranges, since those methods do not attempt mixed-resolution denoising and target different failure modes. The paper would be stronger if it emphasized the mixed-resolution-specific baselines (PI-LR, PI-HR, NTK, PI+NTK, YaRN, RALU, Bottleneck) and treated the generic accelerators as integration experiments.

Several tables have incomplete or inconsistent entries (e.g., the Time column is blank for most baselines in Tabs. 1 and 2, and only 'Ours' rows have times in parts of Tab. 3/4), making the reported efficiency comparisons harder to interpret at a glance.

The theoretical argument in Eq. (6) is essentially the standard observation that RoPE attention scores are a sum of sinusoids in the relative offset, which was already known in the RoPE literature. The novelty is the application to mixed resolution, and the paper could do more to connect this decomposition to the specific cross-resolution failure mechanism (e.g., derive a quantitative bound on phase error for the piecewise-affine remappings in Eq. (4)).

Multi-resolution results (Tabs. 8, 9, 13, 14) rely on external resolution-extrapolation methods (CineScale, DyPE) for baselines as well as for the proposed method, which introduces additional confounds; clearer separation between PMA's effect and these adaptations would help.

The HR baseline in Tab. 1 (DOVER Overall 79.12) still surpasses Ours (75.34), which is consistent with the paper's framing but should be discussed more explicitly as the remaining quality gap. Also, the interpretation that LR queries 'only require coarse context' (Tab. 15) suggests an under-utilized aspect of PMA that deserves more analysis.
